diagnostic_evidence.quote: In most examples one may take $\X \subseteq \R^{d}$ and $\Y \subseteq \R^{k}$

A countable family $\{\varphi_j\}_{j=1}^{\infty} \subset L^{2}(P_X)$ is
\emph{complete} in $L^{2}(P_X)$ if its linear span is dense in
$L^{2}(P_X)$

If $\{\psi_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\subset L^{2}(P_X)$ is complete in the sense
of Definition~\ref{def:complete}, \eqref{eq:orth-char} need only be
verified with $g$ ranging over $\{\psi_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The sentence attaches the qualifier 'under additional hypotheses on P_X' only to radial basis functions and states unconditionally that polynomial, Fourier and wavelet bases are complete in L^2(P_X). In the paper's general setting (X ⊆ R^d, arbitrary P_X with square-integrable Y) this is false: for heavy-tailed P_X polynomials need not even lie in L^2(P_X), and for indeterminate laws (e.g. lognormal) polynomials are in L^2(P_X) but their span is not dense; Fourier and wavelet completeness likewise presuppose a bounded domain or a P_X dominated by Lebesgue measure. Since the residual-orthogonality diagnostic relies on the probe family being complete in L^2(P_X) to reduce (eq:orth-char) to a countable test, the unconditional claim overstates what the method guarantees.

failure_location.quote:
Polynomial bases, Fourier bases, wavelet bases, and---under additional

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the standard hypotheses (e.g. compactly supported P_X, or a moment-determinacy/exponential-moment condition for polynomials; bounded domain or Lebesgue-dominated P_X for Fourier/wavelets) under which these families are complete, and note that the probe-based diagnostic requires such a condition.
issues.overall_effect: The justification that monomial/polynomial probe families suffice to certify f̂_n ≈ m is unsupported for unbounded or heavy-tailed P_X; the experiments (bounded X, bounded L96 attractor) are unaffected.
issues.title: Polynomial (and Fourier/wavelet) bases asserted complete in L^2(P_X) without hypotheses on P_X
issues.why_classification: A short local qualification of hypotheses repairs the claim; no result, rate or experiment is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
The two questions are binary---reducible structure either is or is not
detected, and the residual either is or is not within the task's
tolerance---so together they partition the possibilities into four cases

issues.failure_explanation: The procedure gives two non-equivalent operationalizations of the same decision: 'no probe is both significant and large' (a conjunction) versus 'max_ψ e_n ≤ ε' (effect size alone). Table tab:regimes inherits the mismatch: its 'structure detected' row requires significance AND e_n>ε while its 'no structure detected' row requires only all e_n≤ε, so the case of a probe with e_n>ε that is not significant falls into neither row, contradicting the claim that the two binary questions partition the possibilities into four cases. This case is realizable at the paper's sample sizes: with n=480 diagnostic pairs and ε=0.01, e_n≈0.011 corresponds to |t_n|≈2.2, below the Bonferroni threshold |t|≈3.6, so the two rules give opposite verdicts (barrier reached vs. not).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Choose one criterion (e.g. the effect-size rule max_ψ e_n ≤ ε as the paper's experiments actually use, with significance as a supporting flag) and make the stop rule and the row conditions of tab:regimes consistent with it, including the non-significant/large-effect case.
issues.overall_effect: The decision rule is not well defined in the non-significant, large-effect case, so the classification into Regimes I/I'/II/III and the licensed reading of σ̂_r² as the aleatoric floor is ambiguous there; the reported experiments happen to avoid this case.
issues.title: Stop rule and regime table use incompatible criteria for 'no structure detected'
issues.why_classification: A local rewording aligning the two definitions resolves the ambiguity without changing any theorem, guarantee, or experimental conclusion.
